new_statements.rule_in_words: As reported second-hand for Heine 1976: Nyang'i inherits Proto-Kuliak primary stress unchanged, and that primary stress was not tied to a fixed position (it 'could occur in any position'), i.e. its place is lexically given; a secondary stress falls on the second syllable of the word. This is a tertiary paraphrase of a comparative reconstruction, not a synchronic description of Nyang'i, and it could not be checked against Heine's text.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Second syllable of the word (Proto-Kuliak secondary stress 'remains there in Ik and Nyang'i'), per the same second-hand report.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Schrock 2014:100 adds that 'Tone data on Nyang'ía is not yet available', so it is unknown whether Nyang'i is tonal like Ik or stress-accent like So.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('of a word'); no information on citation forms vs phrases. The only modern description (Beer 2017) rests on one semi-speaker's contracted idiolect (Komol Isaach, Lobalangit, 2012-2014).
new_statements.identity_note: Nyang'i [nyan1313, nyp], Nyangea Mountains / Lobalangit, Karamoja, Uganda; Western Kuliak with Soo/Tepes. No dialect issue, but the sources describe different stages: Heine 1975/1976 worked with the last fluent speakers in the early 1970s, while Beer 2017 documents the contracted idiolect of a single semi-speaker (Komol Isaach, 2012-2014). Any stress statement from Beer 2017 would describe that idiolect.

sources.note: Second-hand paraphrase of Heine 1976: Proto-Kuliak 'primary' stress could occur in any position and remains in place in all Kuliak languages; 'secondary' stress always on the 2nd syllable, remains there in Ik and Nyang'i, shifts to the 1st syllable in Tepes. Also a vowel-correspondence row conditioned on 'Unstressed' position.

sources.note: Comparative morphophonology with a literature survey on Kuliak (Driberg 1932 first wordlist; Heine 1974/75 'recorded almost all that is known'; Weatherby ms. never circulated; Beer 2017 last rememberers). No mention of stress, accent or tone anywhere in the paper.

sources.citation: Schrock, Terrill B. 2014. A grammar of Ik (Icé-tód): Northeast Uganda's last thriving Kuliak language. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (LOT 374). https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/
sources.note: Ik grammar, not Nyang'i; the only Nyang'i prosodic remark is §3.2 Tone, p. 100 (PDF p. 132): 'And from within the Kuliak group, Carlin "found no evidence of So being a tone language" but rather that "stress-accent is important in So..." (1993:16). Tone data on Nyang'ía is not yet available.' Nothing on Nyang'i stress.
No phonology section; nothing on stress or tone. Bibliography lists Beer 2017, Heine 1974-75, Schrock 2017, Driberg 1932, Wiedemann & Nannyombi 2007 without URLs.
